idiom_name: data class copy(...) plus val rebinding (AtomicReference.updateAndGet for shared state)
implementation_notes: Kotlin's update idiom is generated: a data class gets copy(...), which builds a new instance with named overrides, and state is normally held in val properties, so an update is state = state.copy(x = ...) -- the new value is complete before the rebind and a failure inside the constructor or a require() leaves the previous value in place. copy() is shallow, so nested MutableList/MutableMap properties are still shared with the copy; use the read-only collection interfaces and build the new collection with plus/map instead of mutating it in place. The hand-written form is still needed for classes that are not data classes (a withX() method returning a new instance) and for state shared across threads or coroutines, where the commit should be one store -- AtomicReference.updateAndGet or MutableStateFlow.update -- rather than a read-modify-write on a mutable field.
pitfalls: copy() is shallow: a MutableList or MutableMap property is shared with the copy, so a mutation through the copy is visible through the original -- keep state in read-only collection types.

A data class with var properties is not immutable: copy() and with-style updates give no protection against in-place writes, and using such an instance as a map key breaks when a key property changes.
AtomicReference.updateAndGet and MutableStateFlow.update may re-run the lambda, so it must be pure; publishing with plain 'shared.value = ...' from several coroutines loses updates.
